Vocabulary · Lesson 18

Education & study

Talk about your studies like an adult: the course you take, the exam you pass, the degree you want. English fixes each noun to one partner verb, so learn them as chunks: do homework, take a course, pass an exam, get a degree, make progress, sign up for a class. Then sort out three words that many learners confuse: teach, learn, and study.

≈ 55–65 min study collocations teach / learn / study 11 interactive tasks
NoticeRead a student’s message about evening classes.

Say each study chunk aloud: do your homework, take a course, pass an exam, get a degree, make progress, sign up for a class. Keep the noun and its verb together.

Notice before the rule

Read the student’s message

“I take an English course on Tuesday evenings. I always do my homework before class, and last month I passed the first exam. My goal is to get a degree in tourism, so I sign up for a new class every semester. Little by little, I’m making progress.”

  • Look at do my homework. We never say make homework. Which verb goes with homework?
  • Now compare take a course, pass an exam, get a degree. Each noun has one fixed partner verb. Can you find all three?
  • Find making progress. Is progress something you do or something you make?

Discovery check · read the cue, then choose

Each study noun keeps one partner verb. Read the cue in parentheses, then choose the verb English uses.

1You your homework every evening.  (not make)
2I want to a Spanish course next month.  (become a student in it)
3If you study hard, you’ll the exam.  (opposite of fail)
4She works late to good grades.  (earn them)
5Little by little, you progress.  (you get better)
6I’m going to up for evening classes.  (register for them)

The system: teach, learn, or study

Three verbs are easy to confuse. teach is to give knowledge to someone, so a teacher teaches. learn is to receive that knowledge, so a student learns. study is the activity of reading and practicing in order to learn something. You never learn someone; a teacher teaches them.

verbwho does it / meaningexample and past form
teachgive knowledge to someone the teacherThe teacher teaches us grammar.  past: taught
learnreceive knowledge the studentI learn something new in every class.  past: learned
studyread and practice to learn the activityI study for two hours every night.  past: studied

Meaning check

  • You do your homework, never make it. English fixes many study nouns to one verb: do homework, take a course, pass an exam, get a degree, make progress.
  • take, pass, and fail an exam are different steps. First you take an exam (you sit it), then you pass it (you succeed) or fail it (you don’t succeed).
  • School system words: you start elementary school, then high school, then university. A subject is what you study (math, history, science, art, languages). A course runs for one semester and follows a schedule.

Study verbs come in chunks

Learn the verb and its noun together, as one chunk: take a course (become a student in it), pass an exam (succeed) or fail an exam (not succeed), do your homework, get a degree or good grades, make progress, sign up for a class, study for a test.

Say the chunks aloud before the drill. The noun almost never changes its verb, so keep them as a pair.

Drill 1 · choose the study chunk

Read the cue in parentheses first. Each verb fits exactly one sentence.

1I decided to a course in graphic design this fall.  (become a student in it)
2If you review your notes, you’ll the test easily.  (opposite of fail)
3He didn’t open a book all week, so he might the exam.  (not pass it)
4Please your homework before class tomorrow.  (not make)
5After four years, she’ll a degree in biology.  (earn a qualification)
6Practice a little every day, and you’ll progress.  (improve step by step)
7I’m going to up for a cooking class.  (register for it)
8I for two hours every night before a test.  (read and review the material)

Read and choose

A message about evening classes

“Hi Dana! I finally signed up for the Tuesday evening Spanish course at the community college. Classes start next semester and run for twelve weeks. I have to do homework every week and take a short test at the end. I’m a little nervous, but I really want to make progress before our trip to Mexico. Do you want to sign up with me?”

Read, then choose

1. What did the writer sign up for?

2. How long does the course run?

3. Why does the writer want to make progress?

Use it in real life

Your study routine: Say what you are studying now, when you do your homework, and how you review for a test. I’m taking an English course this year. I usually do my homework on Sundays, and I study for a test the night before.
A course you want to take: Choose a subject and explain why. Use sign up for and take a course. I want to sign up for a photography course, because I’d like to take better pictures on my trips.
Ask the teacher: Interview the teacher, then report one answer. What subjects did you like at school? Have you ever taken an online course? Which one do you teach best?
Teach, learn, or study: Say one true sentence with each verb. My father taught me to drive. I’m learning to cook. I study English three times a week.
Your study goal: Plan the next step with be going to. Name the goal, the subject, and one thing you will do to reach it. I’m going to get a degree in nursing. I’m going to sign up for a biology class in September and study every weekend.

Then say one true sentence about what you are studying and one about a study goal for this year.
